items.q:
students(id, name) has 4 rows: 1 Asha, 2 Ravi, 3 Meena, 4 Kiran. fees(student_id, amount) has rows (1, 5000), (1, 2000), (3, 4000).
How many rows does this return?

SELECT s.name, f.amount
FROM students s LEFT JOIN fees f ON f.student_id = s.id;
items.explain: LEFT JOIN keeps every student: Asha appears twice (two fee rows), Meena once, and Ravi and Kiran once each with NULL amount, so 5 rows.

items.q:
orders(city, amount): (Pune, 300), (Pune, 500), (Nagpur, 200), (Nagpur, 100), (Indore, 900).
What does this return?

SELECT city, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM orders
GROUP BY city
HAVING SUM(amount) > 400
ORDER BY total DESC;
options: Indore 900, Pune 800
Pune 800, Indore 900
Indore 900, Pune 800, Nagpur 300
Pune 500, Indore 900
items.explain: HAVING filters groups after aggregation (Nagpur's 300 is dropped), and ORDER BY total DESC puts the larger sum first.

items.q: A query needs only customers who placed at least one order in the last 30 days, using the per-row filter first, then a group condition. Which clause order is valid SQL?
options: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ... HAVING ...
SELECT ... FROM ... GROUP BY ... WHERE ... HAVING ...
SELECT ... FROM ... HAVING ... GROUP BY ... WHERE ...
SELECT ... WHERE ... FROM ... GROUP BY ... HAVING ...
items.explain: WHERE filters rows before grouping, GROUP BY forms the groups, and HAVING filters the groups; the order is fixed in SQL.
COUNT(*) counts all rows, but COUNT(salary) and AVG(salary) ignore NULL, so the average is 150000 / 3.

items.q:
emp(name, city): (A, 'Pune'), (B, NULL), (C, 'Surat').
How many rows does this return?

SELECT name FROM emp
WHERE city != 'Pune' OR city = NULL;
items.explain: Comparing NULL with != or = gives UNKNOWN, which WHERE treats as false, so only C passes; use IS NULL to test for missing values.

items.q: Which query returns the products whose price is above the average price of all products?
options: SELECT name FROM products WHERE price > AVG(price);
SELECT name FROM products WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products);
SELECT name FROM products GROUP BY name HAVING price > AVG(price);
SELECT name, AVG(price) FROM products WHERE price > AVG(price);
items.explain: An aggregate cannot be used directly in WHERE; compute the average once in a scalar subquery and compare each row to it.

items.q:
scores(student, marks): (Asha, 90), (Ravi, 85), (Meena, 90), (Kiran, 70).
What rank does Ravi get?

SELECT student,
  RANK() OVER (ORDER BY marks DESC) AS rnk
FROM scores;
items.explain: RANK leaves gaps after ties: Asha and Meena share rank 1, so the next rank is 3 (DENSE_RANK would give 2).

items.q: You want each employee's salary next to the average salary of their department, without collapsing rows. Which is the right tool?
options: AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept)
AVG(salary) with GROUP BY dept
AVG(salary) in a HAVING clause
DISTINCT dept, AVG(salary)
items.explain: A window function computes the aggregate per partition while keeping every row; GROUP BY would return one row per department.

items.q:
Which query finds customers who have never placed an order? Each option completes:

SELECT c.name FROM customers c ...
options: JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL
WHERE c.id != (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id = NULL
items.explain: A LEFT JOIN keeps customers with no matching order (their order columns are NULL), and IS NULL is the only correct NULL test.

items.q:
sales(region, amount) has 6 rows across 3 regions. What is the row count of this result?

SELECT region, COUNT(*) FROM sales GROUP BY region;
items.explain: GROUP BY returns exactly one row per distinct group, and there are 3 regions.

items.q:
This query fails to run. Why?

SELECT dept, name, MAX(salary)
FROM emp
GROUP BY dept;
options: MAX needs an alias
name is neither grouped nor aggregated
GROUP BY must come before FROM
MAX cannot be used with GROUP BY
items.explain: Every selected column must be in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate, otherwise the database cannot know which name to show for the group.
